idiom_name: pure/ap (liftA2, mapN) over a context; fail-fast vs accumulating instances
implementation_notes:
Language-neutral form: pick the context (value-or-nothing, value-or-error, many values, asynchronous result) and implement two operations - lift a plain value into the context (pure/of) and apply a function-in-context to a value-in-context (ap, equivalently liftA2 or mapN for n arguments). Keep the combining function pure and make the arguments independent: nothing may consume another argument's result, or the construct is a monadic chain wearing applicative clothes. Implement error accumulation as a property of the instance rather than of the call site - combine the error channel with a semigroup/monoid (concatenate lists, join messages) so the same combining code short-circuits with one instance and accumulates with another.

For Scala 3 with Cats: prefer given instances and the `derives` clause for automatic instance derivation. Use `cats.derived.*` for semiauto derivation (recommended over auto for production). For Kotlin Arrow: use `zipOrAccumulate` for accumulating validation across fields and `mapOrAccumulate` for collections; the Raise DSL makes this ergonomic without requiring curried functions. For TypeScript fp-ts: use `E.getApplicativeValidation` with a Semigroup and `sequenceS` for object-shaped combinations; for async use `TE.getApplicativeTaskValidation` with parallel execution.
code_sketch:
# abstract form
pure :: a -> f a                     # lift a plain value into the context
ap   :: f (a -> b) -> f a -> f b      # apply a function in the context
liftA2 f x y = pure(f) `ap` x `ap` y  # combine two independent effects
#   validate_name(user), validate_age(user), validate_email(user)
#   -> liftA3 User  ...            (all errors if the instance accumulates)
#   -> traverse validate fields    (collection of independent checks)

# Haskell: Validation accumulating errors
data Validation e a = Failure e | Success a
instance Semigroup e => Applicative (Validation e) where
  pure = Success
  Success f <*> Success a = Success (f a)
  Failure e1 <*> Failure e2 = Failure (e1 <> e2)  -- accumulate
  Failure e <*> _ = Failure e
  _ <*> Failure e = Failure e

# Scala 3 with Cats: use ValidatedNel for accumulating errors
import cats.data.ValidatedNec
import cats.syntax.all._

case class User(name: String, age: Int, email: String)
def validateUser(name: String, age: String, email: String): ValidatedNec[String, User] =
  (validateName(name), validateAge(age), validateEmail(email)).mapN(User)

# TypeScript fp-ts: accumulating validation with sequenceS
import * as E from 'fp-ts/Either'
import * as NEA from 'fp-ts/NonEmptyArray'
import { getApplicativeValidation } from 'fp-ts/Either'
import { sequenceS } from 'fp-ts/Apply'

const A = getApplicativeValidation(NEA.getSemigroup<string>())
const validateUser = (input: UserInput) =>
  sequenceS(A)({
    name: validateName(input.name),
    email: validateEmail(input.email),
    age: validateAge(input.age)
  })

# Kotlin Arrow: zipOrAccumulate for error accumulation
import arrow.core.zipOrAccumulate
import arrow.core.raise.*

data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)
fun validateUser(name: String, age: String): Either<NonEmptyList<String>, User> =
  either {
    zipOrAccumulate(
      { ensure(name.isNotEmpty()) { EmptyName } },
      { ensure(age.toIntOrNull() != null) { InvalidAge } }
    ) { _, _ -> User(name, age.toInt()) }
  }
pitfalls: Combining arguments that are not actually independent: if one argument's computation uses another's result, the applicative form silently discards that dependency.
Assuming accumulation: the default instance of most error contexts (Either, Result, Task) short-circuits on the first failure - accumulation must be selected explicitly.
Letting the combining function inspect the effects (early returns, exceptions) instead of the values, which breaks the laws the abstraction is supposed to give you.
Using ap on a list Applicative (ZipList) and expecting monadic list behaviour: ZipList's <*> zips positions, it does not sequence as the monad does.
Failing to test law compliance for custom instances: the interchange law in particular is violated by subtle mistakes (e.g., stateful applicatives that discard one argument's effect).

Confusing traverse with sequence: traverse transforms A -> F[B] over a container; sequence reverses the wrapping (F[A] container -> F[container of A]). Both require Applicative but answer different questions.

In Rust, using std::Result::and_then for independent validations silently drops errors after the first failure; a custom Validation type with an accumulating apply method is required for error accumulation.
In Arrow for Kotlin, using `zip` instead of `zipOrAccumulate` short-circuits on the first error; zip is the applicative apply without accumulation semantics.
For fp-ts with Task (async): TE.getApplicativeTaskValidation uses Task's parallel execution by default; ensure you use the correct Apply instance (ApplyPar vs ApplySeq) for the desired semantics.
In Cats Effect, IO itself does not support parallel operations - you must convert to IO.Par via Parallel[IO] and use parMapN/parTupled; regular IO traverse/sequence is sequential.

ZIO's validate/validatePar accumulate errors only within ZIO's Cause type; parallel fibers may not all complete before failure propagates - use ZIO.uninterruptible to ensure all parallel effects complete and report their errors.

Using a bidirectional codec (prismatic/schema, io-ts decode) as a simple validator without understanding its parse/build asymmetry: lenient parsers silently accept malformed input that a strict build cannot round-trip. Enforce canonical forms with a `canonical` guard.
Wrong move: pass a dependent computation to ap or mapN -> it cannot receive the earlier value, so the result uses stale or duplicated input -> instead switch that segment to flatMap or bind.

Wrong move: use the default Either or Result instance expecting every error -> fail-fast semantics discard later failures -> instead select Validated or Validation with a lawful Semigroup error, or collect errors explicitly.

Wrong move: treat ApplicativeDo or Promise.all as proof of parallelism -> runtime scheduling and cancellation remain context-specific -> instead choose an explicit parallel or sequential instance and document its failure and cancellation semantics.

Wrong move: accumulate errors in an unbounded strict list through Validation's <*> -> a failing computation forces every branch, can report thousands of errors to the user, and left-nested chains degrade to quadratic cost (Cheplyaka's benchmark table) -> instead use a lazy or capacity-bounded validator that emits errors incrementally.

Wrong move: treat law-equivalent groupings of an accumulating applicative as runtime-identical -> the laws govern values, not strictness: (f *> f) *> loop differs from f *> (f *> loop) in whether the first collected error can be emitted at all -> instead benchmark the association you actually write whenever laziness or cost matters.

Wrong move: express independent Haxl fetches as monadic do-notation binds -> the runtime cannot start the second fetch until the first result is known, so batching and concurrency are silently lost -> instead bind the fetch results as independent values combined applicatively so the code's shape exposes their independence.

Journal of Functional Programming, 18(1):1–13, 2008. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0956796807006326 — the foundational paper introducing applicative functors (pure and <*>, the four laws) as the structure between Functor and Monad.
https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~ross/papers/Applicative.pdf — PDF of the original McBride-Paterson paper.
https://personal.cis.strath.ac.uk/conor.mcbride/IdiomLite.pdf — an earlier version of the paper with extended examples.

Paolo Capriotti and Ambrus Kaposi. 'Free Applicative Functors.' Haskell Symposium 2014. https://www.paolocapriotti.com/assets/applicative.pdf — defines the FreeA/Ap data type for constructing applicative functors from base functors, enabling static program analysis before interpretation.

Andrey Mokhov, Geoff Clemow, and others. 'Selective Applicative Functors.' Haskell Symposium 2020 / ACM SIGPLAN. https://hackage.haskell.org/package/selective — introduces Selective, an intermediate abstraction between Applicative and Monad that allows static declaration of effects with dynamic selection, enabling static analyzability with conditional execution.

ICFP 2015 / JFP 2018. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0956796818000096 — bridges lens-based and semantic bidirectionalization approaches using applicative-style lifting of bidirectional transformations, guaranteeing well-behavedness by construction.
